title: Chapter XVIII

teacherSummary.text: Wickham is absent from the ball. Elizabeth dances with Darcy and challenges him about Wickham. Her family embarrasses her: Mrs. Bennet boasts loudly of Jane's match, Mary sings badly, and Collins introduces himself to Darcy uninvited.

vocabulary.definition: Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book or essay
vocabulary.context: Her cousin prefaced his speech with a solemn bow, and though she could not hear a word of it, she felt as if hearing it all, and saw in the motion of his lips the words “apology,”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preface”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + fac (Latin facere, "to make, do"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: An object of sport or laughter
vocabulary.context: Darcy, however, should have such an opportunity of ridiculing her relations was bad enough, and she could not determine whether the silent contempt of the gentleman, or the insolent smiles of the ladies, were more intolerable.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ridicule”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact
vocabulary.context: I cannot acquit him of that duty; nor could I think well of the man who should omit an occasion of testifying his respect towards anybody connected with the family.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “testify”: -ify (Latin -ficare, "to make"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: A deeper shade of hauteur overspread his features, but he said not a word, and Elizabeth, though blaming herself for her own weakness, could not go on.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hauteur”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Collins, “were so fortunate as to be able to sing, I should have great pleasure, I am sure, in obliging the company with an air; for I consider music as a very innocent diversion, and perfectly compatible with the profession of a clergyman.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “compatible”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ible (Latin -ibilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (Astron.) An interception or obscuration of the light of the sun, moon, or other luminous body, by the intervention…
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth was the least dear to her of all her children; and though the man and the match were quite good enough for her, the worth of each was eclipsed by Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “eclipse”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To charge with something wrong or disgraceful
vocabulary.context: You will not thank me for detaining you from the bewitching converse of that young lady, whose bright eyes are also upbraiding me.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “upbraid”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The act of choosing, or the state of being chosen
vocabulary.context: And I do not think it of light importance that he should have attentive and conciliatory manners towards everybody, especially towards those to whom he owes his preferment.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preferment”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: She was resolved against any sort of conversation with him, and turned away with a degree of ill humour, which she could not wholly surmount even in speaking to Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “surmount”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth listened with delight to the happy, though modest hopes which Jane entertained of Bingley’s regard, and said all in her power to heighten her confidence in it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “heighten”: ten (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Introductions had strict rules; speaking first to a superior was a breach.

significance: Darcy observes the Bennets' impropriety, which later shapes his advice to Bingley.
discussionQuestions: List each embarrassment and explain how it might affect Jane's prospects.
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVIII,” how does Austen show a disastrous ball? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XVIII, how does Austen develop the idea of a disastrous ball? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVIII develops the idea of a disastrous ball. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XVIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of a disastrous ball. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XVIII suggests about a disastrous ball. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of a disastrous ball. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a disastrous ball responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XVIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a disastrous ball follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XVIII and its treatment of a disastrous ball. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XVIII as evidence for a larger claim about a disastrous ball in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a disastrous ball. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: The act of choosing, or the state of being chosen
To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact

satQuestions.passage: This part of his intelligence, though unheard by Lydia, was caught by Elizabeth, and as it assured her that Darcy was not less answerable for Wickham’s absence than if her first surmise had been just, every feeling of displeasure against the former was so sharpened by immediate disappointment, that she could hardly reply with tolerable civility to the polite inquiries which he directly afterwards approached to make. Attention, forbearance, patience with Darcy, was injury to Wickham. She was resolved against any sort of conversation with him, and turned away with a degree of ill humour, which she could not wholly surmount even in speaking to Mr. Bingley, whose blind partiality provoked her.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XVIII”?
options: A privileged childhood and family love

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: List each embarrassment and explain how it might affect Jane's prospects. No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are prefaced, ridiculing, testifying, hauteur, compatible. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Her cousin prefaced his speech with a solemn bow, and though she could not hear a word of it, she felt as if hearing it all, and saw in the motion of his lips the words “apology,”” Webster's says: Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book or essay. Now the word history: “preface”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + fac (Latin facere, "to make, do"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “ridicule”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “testify”: -ify (Latin -ficare, "to make"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Introductions had strict rules; speaking first to a superior was a breach. Why does this chapter matter? Darcy observes the Bennets' impropriety, which later shapes his advice to Bingley. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a disastrous ball.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: This part of his intelligence, though unheard by Lydia, was caught by Elizabeth, and as it assured her that Darcy was not less answerable for Wickham’s absence than if her first surmise had been just, every feeling of displeasure against the former was so sharpened by immediate disappointment, that she could hardly reply with tolerable civility to the polite inquiries which he directly afterwards approached to make. Attention, forbearance, patience with Darcy, was injury to Wickham. She was resolved against any sort of conversation with him, and turned away with a degree of ill humour, which she could not wholly surmount even in speaking to Mr. Bingley, whose blind partiality provoked her.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XVIII,” how does Austen show a disastrous ball? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a disastrous ball, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes a disastrous ball. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
